title: Cannae: Hannibal’s Perfect Trap
hook: Part 3. How many victories can one invader win before Rome finally breaks?
full_narration: Part 3. How many victories can one invader win before Rome finally breaks? After Trebbia, Hannibal drives his exhausted army through central Italy. [[pause:0.4]] In 217 BCE, fog covers Lake Trasimene as Flaminius follows. Hannibal waits in the hills, and the Roman column enters blind. [[voice:tense]] The trap closes; Rome hears another army vanish on Italian soil. Then Fabius Maximus rises, choosing delay over glorious destruction. [[pause:0.6]] For one year, Rome argues: patience, or one decisive battle. In 216 BCE at Cannae, Rome brings its huge army south. Hannibal bends his center, wraps the flanks, and crushes Roman hope. [[voice:low]] But he cannot storm Rome: walls, exhaustion, and no siege train stop him. Capua defects; southern towns waver, and Philip V of Macedon reaches toward Hannibal. Hannibal gains allies, not surrender; Rome prepares to hunt them. [[pause:0.8]] Follow for part 4.

youtube_description: Part 3 of The Fall of Carthage follows Hannibal after Trebbia, as he pushes deeper into central Italy and sets another trap at Lake Trasimene. Rome turns to Fabius Maximus and his strategy of delay, but patience cannot survive forever. In 216 BCE, Rome risks everything at Cannae, where Hannibal wins his greatest battlefield victory. Yet even after Cannae, Rome does not fall. Its walls, Hannibal’s exhausted army, and the lack of siege support keep the capital standing. Meanwhile, Capua defects, southern Italy wavers, and Philip V of Macedon aligns with Hannibal.
